title: Easy Application of Interleaving in the Classroom
author: Blake Harvard
summary: Blake Harvard, who says he has never written about interleaving in eight years of blogging because it's so difficult to translate into a simple classroom recommendation, highlights a study he says finally cracks that problem. The study, with 155 ninth-through-twelfth-grade students, isolates interleaving's effect from spacing (which usually confounds interleaving research) by giving weekly practice quizzes that mixed blocked and interleaved question formats and testing everything again a month later. Students performed worse on the interleaved quizzes in the short term -- Harvard attributes this to the higher cognitive demand of switching topics -- but on the delayed final test, interleaved items outperformed blocked items in every category, which in turn outperformed non-practiced material. Harvard explains the mechanism via a 'discrimination' account: interleaving forces students to notice the features that distinguish one concept from another, functioning like exposure to non-examples, whereas blocked practice removes the need to discriminate between similar concepts. He closes by praising the study's simplicity and applicability compared to more complex interleaving research designs.
points: The study's key design feature -- reducing the spacing confound that plagues most interleaving research -- lets Harvard credit the delayed-test advantage specifically to interleaving rather than to spacing effects layered on top of it.

Interleaved practice underperformed blocked practice on the immediate end-of-week quizzes but outperformed it on every category of question on the test one month later, an inverted pattern that mirrors the general 'desirable difficulty' finding in cognitive science.

Harvard's mechanistic explanation -- interleaving helps students notice discriminating features between similar concepts, functioning like built-in non-examples -- gives teachers a reason to interleave beyond 'the research says so.'

Harvard explicitly credits the study's simple, non-confounded design as what makes it usable by ordinary classroom teachers, contrasting it with most interleaving research that layers in additional variables.
quotes: Practicing problems (1, 2, 3) of related concepts (A, B, C) in a mixed-up order (A1C1B1C2B2A2B3C3A3).
In general, students actually performed worse on the end of week quizzes that utilized interleaved practice versus blocked practice.
when we look at the final test given a month later, in every instance, students performed better on the questions that were interleaved.
Overall, Interleaved practice > Blocked practice > Non-practice. That is super interesting…but my nerdy self wants to know why.
A leading belief posits that when concepts are interleaved, students are more likely to notice the features that discriminate between concepts, a bit like non-examples.
This study kept it quite simple and teachers can actually pretty easily accommodate for their specific subject, students, and time constraints.
